title: Cone 10 reduction firing schedule
subtitle: A step-by-step firing schedule for stoneware in a gas kiln with reduction atmosphere
excerpt: A cone 10 reduction firing schedule guides a gas kiln from cold through a controlled sequence of temperature rises and reduction periods to a peak of approximately 1280 to 1300°C. Reduction periods are created by restricting air supply to the burners, producing a carbon-rich atmosphere that affects glaze and clay body colour. This tutorial covers the sequence from candling through body reduction and final soak.
sourceNotes: Firing schedule derived from established gas kiln practice; no single proprietary source.

glossaryTerms.definition: A kiln environment in which oxygen is deliberately limited, causing incomplete combustion and forcing carbon monoxide into clay and glaze, which alters colour and surface quality
A small pyramid of ceramic material formulated to bend at a specific temperature, used to assess when a kiln has reached the correct heat work
A slow preheat period at low temperature at the start of a firing to drive off residual moisture from the clay and kiln furniture before temperature is raised

content.text: Gas kiln firing produces carbon monoxide and combustion gases. Fire only in a space with continuous fresh air flow (cross-ventilation, not recirculated air). Never fire with windows fully sealed. Have a carbon monoxide detector in the kiln room. Wear heat-resistant gloves and face shield when peering into the kiln or handling peepholes. Kiln surfaces reach extreme temperatures: keep a clear 1 m zone around the kiln during firing. Have a working fire extinguisher accessible.
A cone 10
reduction atmosphere
firing changes stoneware in ways an electric kiln cannot match. Iron glazes shift from rusty ochres to temmoku blacks based on reduction timing. The schedule below uses
pyrometric cones
and a pyrometer to verify heat work.
Loading
Wax-coat kiln shelf surface and kiln post tips. Place witness cones at multiple levels in the kiln, visible through peepholes. Leave at least 12 mm between pieces for gas circulation.
Stage 1: candling (20 to 200°C, approximately 2 hours)
Candling
drives off moisture. Set burners to minimum with damper fully open. Leave all peepholes open for the first hour. Rise 50°C per hour to 200°C.
Stage 2: oxidation rise (200 to 900°C, approximately 4 to 5 hours)

Increase burner pressure steadily. Keep the damper open to maintain full oxidation (clear flame, no black smoke). Rise at 80 to 100°C per hour. At 573°C, slow the rise slightly to allow the quartz inversion to pass safely.
Stage 3: early body reduction (900 to 980°C, approximately 30 minutes)

Begin light reduction by closing the damper slightly until a small orange flame licks from the peepholes. Maintain this for 30 minutes. This colours the clay body and affects iron-bearing glazes at their most receptive stage.
Stage 4: oxidation recovery (980 to 1100°C, approximately 2 hours)
Open the damper and return to light oxidation. Continue rising at 60°C per hour. This burns off carbon deposited on glaze surfaces while preserving the clay body reduction effect.
Stage 5: late reduction and soak (1100 to cone 10, approximately 2 hours)

At 1100°C, re-enter reduction by closing the damper until a persistent orange flame shows at all peepholes. Hold this reduction as temperature rises to cone 9 bending (around 1260°C on the pyrometer, though atmospheric variation changes this). At cone 9 bending, hold temperature for 20 minutes, then push to cone 10. Soak at cone 10 for 15 to 20 minutes to even the kiln. Turn off burners and close damper to cool.
Troubleshooter

items.problem: Black carbon speckling on glaze surfaces that does not clear by peak temperature
items.cause: Heavy reduction in the early body stage deposited carbon on the glaze before it sealed.
items.fix: Keep early reduction light: just an orange lick at peepholes, not heavy smoke. Allow a longer oxidation recovery to clear carbon before entering late reduction.

items.problem: Cone 10 bending but pieces still look underfired
items.cause: Uneven heat distribution in the kiln: the cone is in a hotter zone and the ware in a cooler one
items.fix: Place witness cones at the top, middle, and bottom of the kiln. Adjust loading to reduce blocking of heat paths. Use a longer soak at cone 10 to even out kiln heat
